articles.title_zh: 60 Minutes Transcript: Donald Trump, the 2026 post-midterm elections interview
articles.content_orig:
This past Tuesday, President Donald Trump's Republican Party suffered an extraordinary midterm repudiation – losing not just the House and Senate, but statewide offices in red states, from Texas to Kansas to South Carolina, that Democrats hadn't won in decades. In the past, this president has met defeat with claims of fraud and the effort to overturn the 2020 election. But when we met with him in the White House on Friday for his first sit-down interview since the midterms, we found him in a surprisingly reflective mood, and seemingly accepting of defeat. Our wide-ranging conversation covered: immigration and corruption, Iran and artificial intelligence, his potential successors and his own mortality. But we began with the election results.
Ross Douthat: Two years ago, you won a big, some might say historic, victory. Just now, the Republican party in the midterms suffered a big, some might say, historic defeat. Give me your political analysis of what just happened.
President Donald Trump: Well, number one, I was not on the ballot. But I campaigned hard for some people. And-- I think if I was on the ballot, it would've been a much different situation because you saw the level of popularity and love. There was love. We had massive rallies. You had to transfer those voters, however, to candidates that they didn't like. But there's something beyond that. They didn't like the war. They didn't like the fact that gasoline went up, 'cause I had it down at a low, and there's-- a great dislike, incredibly, for Israel.
Ross Douthat: Let's go through those then one by one.
President Donald Trump: Go ahead.
Ross Douthat: Start-- start with the candidates, right? You said it was tough to transfer your own appeal to candidates
President Donald Trump: Yeah.
Ross Douthat: But in a lot of cases, you picked the candidates. You endorsed Ken Paxton--
President Donald Trump: Well, I--
President Donald Trump: I--
Ross Douthat: He had a tough time.
President Donald Trump: Sure.
Ross Douthat: You endorsed Darline Graham--
President Donald Trump: But-- but Cornyn--
Ross Douthat: --in South Carolina.
President Donald Trump: --Cornyn would've lost also. Darline, I did that in-- honor of a man named Lindsey, who was a friend of mine. And she fought hard. She fought hard. She really did.
Ross Douthat: She lost a very Republican state.
President Donald Trump: Oh--
Ross Douthat: To a very liberal challenger--
President Donald Trump: I won-- I won South Carolina by the highest vote in history by far. I won Texas by the highest vote in history by far. I won Florida who, by the way, I did endorse. And he's gonna be-- a great governor and a great senator. I endorsed both of them. And, had I not endorsed them, they wouldn't have won.
Ross Douthat: Why can't it transfer? You-- you were out on the trail, and you said--
President Donald Trump: It didn't transfer--
Ross Douthat: You said, "Vote like I'm on the ballot."
President Donald Trump: Yeah. It didn't--
Ross Douthat: And people didn't? Or-- or did they? Did they vote because they were mad at you--
President Donald Trump: No, they--
President Donald Trump: I think they didn't vote, really. I think in some cases, they didn't like the candidates. And that's, you know, their prerogative.
Ross Douthat: Couple days ago your vice president, JD Vance, wrote a social media post where he says, "The reason we lost is the war," meaning Iran. And he said things in that post--
President Donald Trump: I don't disagree--
Ross Douthat: About Israel. Yeah. So you agree with his analysis?
President Donald Trump: I don't disagree with it
Ross Douthat: Did you know he was gonna write that post?
President Donald Trump: He asked me what do I think. I said, "You write what you're--" I said--
Ross Douthat: "Write what you--"
President Donald Trump: You write what you want--"
Ross Douthat: "Write what you feel"?
President Donald Trump: By the way, "What are you gonna write? "The only thing I wish he would've said there, if he felt it, and you'd have to ask him about that, but if you had to do it again, would you do it? You know, he's part of a decision-making process. And my answer is an emphatic yes because you can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon. I think, historically, this will be a very good decision. Is it a good decision for today and tomorrow? Maybe not. But you know, I have to go with what's right for our country. If they had a nuclear weapon during my term, I would be excoriated far worse than what's happened. So--
Ross Douthat: All right. Let's-- let's--
President Donald Trump: I've stopped--
President Donald Trump: But Ross, I've stopped them from having a nuclear weapon. That's a big thing.
The president argued that even with the Iran war, the U.S. economy in his second term has been very strong.
Ross Douthat: But in poll after poll, people say they're unhappy with this economy in a way they weren't in the first term. Cost of living, inflation, and so on. Is that all just the Iran war?
President Donald Trump: Well, it's not really the Iran war because the numbers are phenomenal. I think it was bad messaging, maybe by me, but I would talk about it all the time. So I don't know, how much can I talk about it? Look, the press doesn't cover-- positive news for Republicans. They don't cover certainly positive news for me. So I have to do it myself. I have to get it out there. We have historically good numbers. We have the highest stock market in history.
Ross Douthat: But why don't Americans feel it, that--
President Donald Trump: They don't--
Ross Douthat: Why-- why don't they-- 'cause they're--
President Donald Trump: Because I think--
Ross Douthat: Obviously, like, you and the press, you and the media, you and our business have been in tension throughout your career.
President Donald Trump: Correct.
Ross Douthat: But you still won elections, right?
President Donald Trump: Yeah.
Ross Douthat: So why couldn't you win this time--
President Donald Trump: I think it was bad messaging.
Ross Douthat: What was the bad message?
President Donald Trump: We couldn't get the word across.
Whether it was the message or the record, the Republican collapse will give Democrats in Congress new powers over budgets, hearings, and subpoenas.
Ross Douthat: You came out after the midterms. You congratulated the Democrats.
President Donald Trump: Correct.
Ross Douthat: You said that you were open to working with them.
President Donald Trump: True.
Ross Douthat: What is one thing you would like to work with a Democratic majority on--
President Donald Trump: I'd love to do something on immigration.
President Donald Trump: Because-- well, so
Ross Douthat: Do you think immigration hurt you in the midterms?
President Donald Trump: I think--
Ross Douthat: Do you think the crackdown hurt you--
President Donald Trump: I think it both helped and hurt. I think I got an A+ for closing up the border. I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out. But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that-- that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally. Now, there is a large part of the country that think that they should be put out. And there's a large part of the country that think that they should be allowed to stay if they're good people working in a landscaping company, or workin' in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases, paying taxes. And there's a large group of people who think that they should be allowed to stay.
Ross Douthat: So you think your deportation policy--
President Donald Trump: I think it was--
Ross Douthat: Went too far--
President Donald Trump: Too tough.
Ross Douthat: It was too tough?
President Donald Trump: I think it might be too tough, yeah.
Ross Douthat: What would--
President Donald Trump: And-- and I think--
Ross Douthat: What does a deal look like
President Donald Trump: I think ultimately--
Ross Douthat: With the Democrats?
President Donald Trump: That hurt me. We

articles.title_orig: Trump’s proposed Russia deal raises NATO alarm as ex-commander warns Putin seeks influence over Europe
articles.title_zh: Trump’s proposed Russia deal raises NATO alarm as ex-commander warns Putin seeks influence over Europe
articles.content_orig:
Retired Gen. Philip Breedlove warns any deal meeting Russia's demands could face European resistance.
President Donald Trump's push for a deal with Russia to end the war in Ukraine and potentially reshape European security has raised alarm among NATO allies, with a former top alliance commander warning Fox News Digital that President Vladimir Putin has long sought to divide the world into competing spheres of influence.
The warning came as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also appeared to reject what he called a potential "Yalta 2.0," and NATO allies debated direct outreach to Putin ahead of delegations preparing for talks in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11.
Retired Gen. Philip Breedlove , the former Supreme Allied Commander Europe, warned that Putin's ambitions extend far beyond Ukraine and reflect a broader vision for how global powers should divide influence.
"Putin has a plan for the world, and he has pushed that plan on leaders several times," Breedlove warned before adding: "He talks about it and he writes about it."
ZELENSKYY TO SEEK OFFRAMP FOR YEARS-LONG RUSSIA WAR IN UN SPEECH AFTER TRUMP REVEALS PEACE DEAL IS CLOSE
Finnish President Alexander Stubb, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, French President Emmanuel Macron, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, front row from left, and Jonas Gahr Støre, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Ursula von der Leyen, Dutch Prime Minister Dick Schoof, and Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson, back row from left, stand together in the chancellery in Berlin, Germany, on Dec. 15, 2025. (Markus Schreiber, Pool/AP)
Trump had suggested Thursday that an agreement with Moscow could extend beyond ending Russia's nearly five-year war in Ukraine.
"It's going to be a big agreement, and it's going to involve more than Ukraine... I could even say it might involve all of Europe," Trump told reporters after meeting Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev at the White House.
"It's going to be a big, beautiful agreement, and everyone's going to be thrilled," Trump added.
Breedlove said Putin has repeatedly promoted a vision of dividing global power among Russia, China and the United States.
"The plan is three spheres of influence whereby China controls the Far East, Russia controls Europe, and America controls the Western Hemisphere. I do not expect there's going to be a lot of cooperation from the countries of Europe," he said.
"The Western world is waiting to see what this big plan is, and they are very concerned because it is about them," Breedlove added.
President Donald Trump (R) and Russian President Vladimir Putin (L) hold a meeting at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson on August 15, 2025 in Anchorage, Alaska. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
Zelenskyy also warned Friday against repeating the 1945 Yalta Conference , where Allied leaders negotiated Europe's postwar order before the Soviet Union consolidated control over Eastern Europe.
"We don't want to have Yalta 2.0," the Ukrainian leader told CNN . "We don't want to be divided by Russia," he said before adding: "For me, it's not simple and it can be dangerous."
On Sunday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters that discussions on how Europe would look after the Ukraine war were already underway.
"It's one of the key topics that's been raised repeatedly in every conversation, anytime negotiations have been discussed," he said ahead of traveling to Paris for the G7 meeting.
RUBIO SOUNDS CAMPAIGN-READY AS HE RAILS AGAINST OPEN BORDERS, GLOBALISM IN SPEECH FROM ANCIENT GREEK RUINS
Secretary of State Marco Rubio talks to reporters at NATO Headquarters in Brussels, Belgium, on Friday, April 4. (Jacquelyn Martin/Pool/AP)
"So I think that's what the president is alluding to, is that there's been some advances made and what that architecture could look like post-conflict. We obviously have to get past the conflict to get to that point," he added, clarifying Trump's comments.
Breedlove, however, questioned whether European governments and Ukraine would even accept a broader agreement negotiated without their involvement.
"I do expect that when we get a peek under the hood of what Mr. Putin and Mr. Trump have devised that there may be European partners and allies to include Ukraine that may or may not be enthralled with the proposed solution."
"We have always said nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine," the expert said.
"Neither have we heard anything about the EU or NATO being in this conversation. And yet the EU, NATO and Ukraine are central and the heart of the matter that apparently is going to be discussed."
Tensions also appeared to mount further after Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre held a rare 90-minute telephone conversation with Putin on Oct. 27, according to reports .
TRUMP NEGOTIATORS WITKOFF, KUSHNER MEET WITH PUTIN IN MOSCOW AS US PUSHES FOR END TO RUSSIA-UKRAINE WAR
A composite image shows Russian President Vladimir Putin (L) and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy (R) as peace talks continue. (Valery Sharifulin/Pool/AFP via Getty Images; Sean Gallup/Getty Images)
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen criticized the separate European diplomatic initiatives.
"I think Europe should stick together rather than going solo," she said as Breedlove went on to defend the outreach.
"The two calls that recently took place between Northern leaders in the NATO alliance and Russia, I don't think that they're out of place at all," he said. "I think they're entirely appropriate."
"The great powers of Europe are getting very concerned that someone is dealing with their security without including them in the conversation," he added.
Meanwhile, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot confirmed Sunday that France would participate in the Abu Dhabi negotiations.
"The Europeans will be well represented; France will be in Abu Dhabi to take part in these discussions," Barrot said, according to Reuters.
FORMER UK PRIME MINISTER TONY BLAIR WARNS EUROPE ‘WE DON’T WIN’ IN WAR WITHOUT US SUPPORT
President Donald Trump speaks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, as they meet to negotiate for an end to the war in Ukraine, at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson in Anchorage, Alaska, U.S., August 15, 2025. (Kevin Lamarque/Reuters)
Breedlove warned that any agreement requiring European nations to sacrifice their security to satisfy Moscow would still face fierce resistance.
"If the maximalist demands of Russia remain intact and in order to find peace, all the rest of Europe has to give up its security, sacrifice its security, make itself more susceptible to Russian attack, then this is not going to go well," he said.
"Putin has never been a partner for peace in Ukraine. Putin is not now a partner for peace in Ukraine."
"The EU nations, the NATO nations, and Ukraine are not going to sign up to a plan that suggests that Russia will be able to once again amass its armies, march across borders and intervene in its neighbors' internal business."

"We need to understand that we are in a war. Mr. Putin is at war with the West," he warned.
Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

articles.title_orig: Newport Beach fishermen find Royal Caribbean cruise ship employee treading water 20 miles off coast
articles.title_zh: Newport Beach fishermen find Royal Caribbean cruise ship employee treading water 20 miles off coast
articles.content_orig:
Two Newport Beach fishermen found a Royal Caribbean cruise ship employee treading water nearly 20 miles off the coast while returning home from a fishing trip near Catalina Island on Friday.
Sean Norton and Grant Garrett were fishing for marlin in the morning. By noon, they had rescued the 37-year-old man who had been treading water nearly 20 miles off the coast in the middle of the Pacific Ocean.
"I'm like, 'Yeah, it's a human being. Stop the boat; let's get all of our lines in," Garrett said, recalling the moment the boat's captain spotted the man in the water.
"Grant and I each got an arm and lifted him up," Norton said. "He was in total shock."
Garrett said when the man came to, he told them he was a pianist on the 14-deck Royal Caribbean cruise ship called the "Ovation of the Seas," which was en route to Ensenada, Mexico out of Long Beach.
"The only thing he said to me was, 'Thank you. I thought I was gonna die,'" Norton said.
After pulling him from the water, the crew put out an emergency maritime call, and a group of Newport Beach lifeguards responded to help.
"It was approximately 15 to 20 miles offshore, pretty much in the middle of the ocean," Battalion Chief Adam Yacenda said. They believe he may have gone overboard from the ship about nine hours before he was found, at around 2:30 a.m.
The man, who still hasn't been identified, was hospitalized after the ordeal and is expected to survive, according to the U.S. Coast Guard, which is investigating the incident and how he went overboard.
"You have this crazy super El Niño year. This guy was in the water for probably 10 hours, but the water's 76 degrees," Norton said. "A different year, no way he makes it."
In a statement to CBS LA, a Royal Caribbean Group spokesperson shared, "We are providing support and assistance to our crew member during this difficult time. To respect the privacy of our employee, we have no additional details to share."

articles.title_orig: Europeans will join Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi, French foreign minister says
articles.title_zh: Europeans will join Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi, French foreign minister says
articles.content_orig:
A view through the destroyed walls of a kindergarten shows a large bomb crater and a damaged residential apartment building following a missile attack in Kyiv, Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026. Dan Bashakov/AP hide caption
European officials will turn up for the U.S.-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine in the United Arab Emirates this week, France's foreign minister said Sunday, days after the Kremlin had insisted there could be no role for European powers at the meeting.
"France will be there and will ensure that Europe's voice is heard," Jean-Noël Barrot told French radio. He did not say who would represent Paris, or whether French or other European officials would take part directly in negotiations, or simply observe.
The meetings, which are set to take place in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday, had previously been presented as a three-way session between Washington, Moscow and Kyiv.
The Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov had earlier ruled out a European role, saying the trilateral format had already been agreed.
Talking to a Russian news channel on Friday, he accused European governments of failing to decide who speaks for them, while acknowledging that security talks would at some point require Europe's involvement.
On Thursday, President Trump met Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev and said a coming agreement was "going to involve more than Ukraine," adding he could even say it "might involve all of Europe."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told CNN on Friday that he had not been given details of the agreement Trump had referenced, and warned: "For me, it's not simple, and it can be dangerous." He invoked the 1945 Yalta conference, where Allied leaders settled Europe's division without the involvement of several affected countries.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, right, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy attend a press conference in Berlin, Germany, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. Ebrahim Noroozi/AP hide caption
This will be the fourth round of talks between the two warring nations brokered by the Trump administration, and the first since those in Geneva this February. Earlier U.S.-brokered meetings have made little progress, and the chances of a breakthrough have been reduced as the Trump administration focused on its war with Iran.
Moscow confirmed it would return to the negotiating table only following a visit by U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg in October. Those talks saw Putin announce the release of an American prisoner from a Russian jail — an apparent Kremlin gesture to President Trump's earlier lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel exports. Ukraine was vehemently opposed to the fuel sales — arguing they helped replenish Moscow's war chest.
Witkoff has said the agenda for these latest talks will include postwar security arrangements and de-escalation of the conflict and humanitarian issues, shortly after Melania Trump helped broker a limited ceasefire that allowed humanitarian aid to enter a town inside Russian-occupied Ukraine.
Russia's delegation will again be led by Vladimir Medinsky, a hardline Putin aide who has participated in most talks with Ukraine since the unsuccessful first set of discussions all the way back in March 2022.
For the first time, these talks will also include Deputy Foreign Ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, as well as Yury Zhigarlovsky, a deputy head of the General Staff's operations directorate, alongside military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov.
This more senior lineup could indicate that Moscow is readier than before to address thorny political and military questions. But the U.S. think tankInstitute for the Study of War suggested some of those same Russian officials have in fact previously sought to slow down previous talks or push harder on Moscow's demands.
The gaps between the two countries remain substantial. Russia has demanded that Ukraine give up large parts of its territory and renounce NATO membership. Zelenskyy has repeatedly insisted any security commitments should be clearly spelled out, including who would act, and how, if Russia attacked again.
Russian President Vladimir Putin, right, interacts with people at the monument to merchant Kuzma Minin and Prince Dmitry Pozharsky, leaders of the struggle against foreign invaders in 1612, in Red Square in Moscow, Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026, during National Unity Day celebrations. Yuri Kochetkov/Pool Sputnik Kremlin hide caption
Some analysts expect little. In an op-ed for the Atlantic Council think tank, the former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine John Herbst argued that Putin had rejected every U.S. proposal Kyiv accepted and preferred participating in peace talks than pursuing actual peace. "Perhaps the only outcome of the talks," he wrote, "will be to agree to another round."
The meetings in the United Arab Emirates also follow Democrats' midterm victories, which Zelenskyy said could improve Ukraine's chances of more U.S. aid.
Russia, too, may be looking to push for the Trump administration's outlines of a Ukraine deal — before a Democratic-controlled Congress arrives come January.
Also hovering over the talks — the prospect of Trump, Xi, and Putin gathering for a trilateral meeting at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China later this month. While details remain murky, all sides have confirmed discussions are underway.
And as officials travel to Abu Dhabi to talk peace, the war has raged on regardless.
Zelenskyy said Russia fired 36 ballistic missiles at the Kyiv area overnight Saturday, with only four intercepted, accusing Moscow of treating diplomacy "as a form of aggression."
In southern Ukraine, the death toll from a guided-bomb strike Monday on an aid distribution site in Komyshuvakha rose to at least 55.

articles.title_orig: Train crash kills seven, injures dozens near Egypt’s Cairo city
articles.title_zh: Train crash kills seven, injures dozens near Egypt’s Cairo city
articles.content_orig:
At least seven people have been killed and more than 125 others injured in a train crash on the outskirts of Cairo in Egypt’s Giza province, according to the country’s Health Ministry.
A train travelling between Giza and Fayoum on Sunday ran into the back of another train on the Cairo-to-Aswan route, causing the latter to derail from its tracks onto a countryside road in the district of al-Ayyat, authorities said.
Emergency rescue teams and cranes were dispatched to the scene to clear the wreckage and restore train services to their normal schedule as soon as possible, Egyptian National Railways said.
Authorities say more than 70 ambulances were involved in transport and evacuation operations at the scene of the crash, with casualties taken to nearby hospitals.
President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi said he was following the accident “with great concern”, and had directed authorities to conduct an urgent investigation to “hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent”.
Witnesses described chaotic rescue efforts after the collision, as villagers, first responders and railway workers scrambled to reach passengers trapped inside overturned carriages.
Abdel Wahed Mohamed, 31, who was sitting at a nearby cafe when the collision occurred, said the Aswan-bound train had stopped, when the Fayoum-bound train crashed into it.
“The train overturned at around 1:30 pm [11:30 GMT]. Six carriages overturned,” he said, adding that victims suffered a range of injuries, including head wounds and broken limbs.
Another witness, Ahmed Moussa, 25, said rescuers dug beneath one overturned carriage to reach trapped passengers.
“There were people piled on top of each other inside,” he said, adding that he saw two women among the dead.
Taha Abdel Tawab, 43, said he “saw a young man leaving the train carrying his dead father”.
Al-Ayyat district, where the collision happened, is also the site of Egypt’s worst-ever rail disaster .
In 2002, more than 370 people were killed when a fire swept through a train carrying holiday travellers south of Cairo. In 2009, multiple train crashes in the area killed dozens.
Egypt’s 110 million people depend heavily on rail transport, but the cross-country network – one of the largest in Africa – is in need of modernisation.
Over the past decade, Egypt has poured billions of dollars into updating its transport infrastructure, including new highways and high-speed rail lines, but has yet to overhaul much of its dated train services .

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to having an affair with a woman whom U.S. intelligence reportedly suspects is a Chinese spy.
Huang, who heads a leading AI chipmaker and is an ally of President Donald Trump , apologized in a message to the company, saying, “I was unfaithful to my wife,” according to The New York Times .
“My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”
Nvidia announced in a press release Sunday that its board was opening an independent investigation “in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”
Late last month, the Times reported that Huang had formed a close relationship with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese executive at a Singapore-based data center.
Alice Huang is considered by U.S. officials to be a Chinese spy, feeding information to Beijing, according to the report, which cited sources briefed on the surveillance of Alice Huang and other officials and industry experts.
“The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” Sunday’s company press release read.
“While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information.”
CEO Huang supports the investigation and has agreed to cooperate with it, the board said.
There was no word of Huang’s position being in jeopardy, with the board saying it “has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team.”
Nvidia is one of the hottest companies in the stock market right now, given the popularity of its chips. It has a market capitalization of roughly 4.5 trillion and was trading at nearly $240 per share early last month.
Huang, like other tech leaders, has flocked to Trump as the president embraces AI. The Nvidia leader and his wife, Lori Huang, attended a state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House in September. His attendance wasn’t unusual, given that OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg were also there.

articles.title_zh: Netanyahu rival Eisenkot tapped to form Israeli government
articles.content_orig:
Nov. 8 (UPI) -- Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot said he is open to including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the coalition he is working to build.
Eisenkot, who has been tasked with forming the country's next government by President Isaac Herzog, also suggested far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich would be welcomed to join.
"If members of Likud and the Religious Zionist Party truly believe this is a time for unity, as they told the president, I cannot conceive of any reason why they would not support a government under my leadership and the principles I have presented," Eisenkot said.
Eisenkot, who has six weeks to form a new government , said he would represent all segments of Israeli society.
Meanwhile, Herzog said Israel faces uncertainties after the U.S. midterm elections last week, which saw several candidates critical of Israel and military support by Washington win seats in the U.S. Senate and House.
"The State of Israel needs a stable government," Herzog said, citing a "new political reality" in the U.S.
Eisenkot was the head of the Israeli military from 2015 to 2019 and served as an observer in Netanyahu's war cabinet for the first eight months of the country's war on Gaza after the Hamas attacks on Israel in October 2023.
Still, Arab-led parties have endorsed Eisenkot to replace Netanyahu.
In Israel's election last month, Eisenkot's alliance of four parties won 48 seats in parliament, while Netanyah's right-wing and religious bloc took 53 seats. Each missed the 61 seats needed for a majority. Arab-led parties won 19 seats, a record.
Eisenkot has rejected forming a government with the Arab-led parties, even though it would give him a bloc of 67 seats. He would secure 61 seats by winning over two ultra-religious parties, United Torah Judaism and Shas.
Eisenkot may be able to form a government with less than 61 votes by winning a confidence vote in parliament.

Sequoia Capital announced some major changes this week, including the closure of its London office, the merger of its early-stage and growth teams, and the end of its Scouts program .
Now, the Financial Times has published a report painting all of this as an attempt to undo the legacy of former leader Roelof Botha, who stepped down as the firm’s steward last year . An unnamed source told the FT that Botha “loved process and hierarchy,” while “the rest of the team didn’t.”

articles.title_orig: China's half-price Rolls-Royce: Yangwang Altior is a lavish alternative to a Phantom limo
articles.title_zh: China's half-price Rolls-Royce: Yangwang Altior is a lavish alternative to a Phantom limo
articles.content_orig:
By ROB HULL, MOTORING EDITOR
Updated: 13:34 EDT, 8 November 2026
We've had the Temu Range Rover; now there's an AliExpress Roller.
Chinese brand Yangwang, a spin-off from electric car giant BYD, has unveiled a new battery-powered luxury vehicle called the Altior, and it bears a striking resemblance to the iconic British Rolls-Royce Phantom limousine – but for around half the price.
At 5.6m long, with a vast bonnet and grille, rear-hinged coach doors, a palatial interior and umbrellas stowed inside the door panels, there's no hiding which ostentatious motor it has firmly set its sights on.
Altior means 'higher' in Latin, with the car 'expressing an ambition to elevate the experience of luxury through cultural depth, personal expression and technological progress', Yangwang says.
Just 399 are going to be produced and reports in China suggest pre-orders are available from 2million yuan, which equates to around £230,000.
That puts it closer to the £250,000 Rolls-Royce Ghost than the flagship £450,000 Phantom, though that's before taking into account heavily subsidised pricing in China's domestic market.
Its global premiere in Abu Dhabi this weekend comes just days after car registration figures revealed that Jaecoo's 'Temu Range Rover' 7 SUV was the UK's best-selling new model for a second successive month .
The runaway success of the Range Rover Velar lookalike is the clearest sign yet that Chinese brands are coming for the old guard of established luxury carmakers. And with the Altior, it appears not even Rolls-Royce is safe.
This is the new Yangwang Altior limousine - a luxury Rolls-Royce Phantom rival from Chinese EV giant, BYD
While the Rolls-Royce Phantom and Ghost feature a gutsy 6.75-litre twin-turbocharged V12 petrol engine, the Yangwang Altior is a far greener proposition.
It uses a version of the quad-electric motor setup deployed in the Chinese firm's other models, the U8 SUV and U9 supercar. That's likely to produce more than 1,000bhp and will allow it to perform a tank turn , rotating each wheel independently to spin the vehicle on its own axis.
Providing the energy for the e-motors is BYD's second-generation Blade Battery technology.
As such, it's claimed to be capable of travelling more than 621 miles on a full charge. However, this is based on Chinese efficiency tests that are historically a shade more optimistic than Europe's cycle, which would be closer to 520 miles.
The battery is compatible with BYD's network of Flash Charging stations, of which there are 10,000 already in China and a promise to install 300 here in the UK .
The ground-breaking devices can deliver up to 1,500kW of power and top up a battery pack from 10 to 70 per cent charge in as little as five minutes, before reaching full charge in less than ten.
That's not all in terms of technological advances.
The Yangwang boasts a suite of chassis tech that means it can float if there are flash floods or the driver 'accidentally enters water'. And it can continue tracking in a straight line when one of the tyres suffers a high-speed blowout on the motorway.
The Altior also taps into BYD's God's Eye A assisted-driving system, which includes parking-space-to-parking-space navigation assistance. This enables the car to drive itself from one car park to another, even when they are hundreds of miles apart.
The suspension is clever too. The brand's DiSus active body control system uses cameras to read the road ahead and adjusts damping in real time, meaning occupants won't feel potholes or changes in road surfaces while stretched out in the back.
Altior means 'higher' in Latin, as BYD's spin-off Yangwang looks to enter a more opulent market with its latest model. And it certain strikes a resemblance to the Rolls-Royce Phantom
Squint slightly and there's no mistaking the Rolls-Royce-inspired silhouette.
The elongated bonnet, despite there being no 12-cylinder combustion engine lurking beneath it, and the glitzy upright grille are trademarks of the 122-year-old British marque.
The Altior's front end is described as a 'masterpiece of high jewellery'.
'Meticulous selection, polishing and individual placement create a composition that responds to changing light, revealing new depth and brilliance as the viewpoint moves,' the Chinese manufacturer says.
Its lights are a little special too, featuring 12 individual elements that rotate from the outside to the centre to create a 'ceremonial welcome' when the owner approaches.
At 5.6m long, the Altior (pictured left) is 5.5cm longer than the Ghost and 16cm shorter than the Phantom (pictured right)
Like all Roller limousines, the Chinese Yangwang has rear-hinged coach doors
Twenty-one-inch wheels are standard, with the dish-style monoblock design bearing more than a passing resemblance to the disc rims available on a Phantom
Is it time for European luxury car makers to fear China’s fast-rising electric rivals?
At 5.6m long, the Altior is 5.5cm longer than the Ghost and 16cm shorter than the Phantom.
However, the Yangwang's other dimensions, including a width of 2m, a height of almost 1.6m and a wheelbase of 3.5m, are almost like-for-like with the bigger of the two Rolls-Royces.
Twenty-one-inch wheels are standard, with the dish-style monoblock design bearing more than a passing resemblance to the disc rims available on a Phantom.
The doors also open in the fashion for which Rolls-Royce is famed, providing generous access to the opulent interior.
The finely crafted bespoke umbrellas hidden in each door panel, much like those in a Rolls-Royce, are said to be inspired by the circular wooden roof of the Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests at China's Temple of Heaven complex.
The cockpit is the least Roller-like part of the car. While the British luxury firm attempts to conceal tech for a traditional look, the Yangwang has a dashboard-wide high-definition screen
Exactly like Rolls-Royces, though, the Chinese limo has bespoke, hand-crafted umbrellas hidden in a compartment within the doors
Step inside and the cabin – dubbed a 'private lounge' – is awash with only the highest-quality materials.
These include hammer-tested metal switches, pure-wool floor mats, real-wood veneers, 48 jewellery-inspired control buttons and semi-aniline leather upholstery.
The designers have even mounted polished yellow jade gemstones inside the vertical air vents, while the silk-embroidered door panels feature cloud and thunder-pattern motifs.
The cockpit itself looks a little less Rolls-Royce-esque, even if it does feature a chrome-rimmed steering wheel wrapped in beautifully finished leather.
While the British car maker generally tries to subtly conceal much of its modern technology up front, the Yangwang has a dashboard-spanning digital glass display. This incorporates an instrument cluster with classic-style digital dials and an enormous infotainment screen featuring a laptop-style taskbar of icons.
But it's the rear compartment that well-heeled customers will want to know about.
The cabin is as palatial as you'd expect from a Rolls-Royce or Bentley limo. It boasts aviation-style zero-gravity seats, real-wood veneers and 48 jewellery-inspired control buttons
There's a fridge in the rear and in the front, two champagne flute holders and a control panel that means you won't have to converse with your chauffeur at all
There's plenty of artistry too. Silk-embroidered door panels feature cloud and thunder-pattern motifs
The four-seat layout is almost perfectly symmetrical and 'gives each occupant a clearly defined personal space' where the owner in the back can feel entirely separate from Jeeves behind the wheel by elevating a divider between them.
Owners won't need to ask their chauffeur for anything, either.
Rear occupants can access all key functions through the central console, including lowering the front passenger seat at the touch of a button to provide an uninterrupted view ahead.

articles.title_orig: King leads solemn Remembrance Sunday service at Cenotaph
articles.title_zh: King leads solemn Remembrance Sunday service at Cenotaph
articles.content_orig:
King Charles III led the nation in a solemn two-minute silence on Remembrance Sunday in London to honour veterans who had died in conflict.
On a stone-grey autumn morning, he laid a wreath at the Cenotaph in Whitehall before a march-past by 10,000 armed forces veterans.
That included a shrinking number of World War Two veterans, with 12 taking part this year, including 103-year-old Annie Duplock, who described it as a "very emotional day".
Meanwhile, the number of former prime ministers reached a record high, with nine lined up to lay wreaths, while Andy Burnham attended for the first time as the current occupant of No 10 Downing Street.
And for the first time, the leader of Reform UK, Nigel Farage, had enough MPs in Parliament to qualify to lay a wreath alongside other major party leaders.
The Prince of Wales and the Princess Royal were among royals in attendance, along with military chiefs, senior politicians, diplomats and faith leaders, watched by big crowds squeezed behind railings along Whitehall.
Queen Camilla and the Princess of Wales watched from a balcony above the Cenotaph in the Foreign Office.
Among the flags on the roof of that Whitehall building was the Ukrainian blue and yellow. It went up when Russia invaded and four years later it is now visibly frayed - a reminder of the length of that war and of current threats.
At 11:00 GMT, as the first strike of Big Ben echoed from the nearby Houses of Parliament, the big two-minute silence filled the usually frenetic streets, before the playing of the Last Post.
The King had his eyes closed, the crowds in Whitehall stopped for their own thoughts, in a rare moment of calm in the capital.
The poignant parade past the Cenotaph included representatives of about 340 different military and civilian groups, from the Royal Naval Association and the Royal Marines Association to Transport for London and the Royal National Lifeboat Institute.
Alongside those marching were flotillas of disability scooters and families helping veterans in wheelchairs.
Those who took part in WW2 are now increasingly frail - and there were 12 participants in the march-past compared to 20 last year. The oldest participant this year was aged 105.
Taking part for the first time was 103-year-old Annie Duplock, who had been part of the Land Army that had helped to feed the country at war.
She had joined the Land Army in 1940 as a 16-year-old, having lied about her age, and worked on a farm in Leicestershire.
"I feel very honoured to be taking part in the parade and to represent the Land Girls. I'm very excited, although a little apprehensive as I don't quite know what to expect," she said.
"I think it will be a very emotional day, bringing back memories of all those who didn't return home. It will be lovely to be there and remember them."
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the annual event was a time to "reflect on the selflessness and courage it takes to commit your life to protecting others".
He earlier announced that he wanted to tackle the problem of homelessness among ex-service personnel to "ensure that any veteran sleeping rough is offered appropriate accommodation before Christmas".
Mark Atkinson, the director general of the Royal British Legion, said: "As we come together on Remembrance Sunday, we pay tribute to all those who have served and sacrificed, from generations past to those still serving today."
Remembrance events took place across the country as thousands gathered to pay their respects to those who died in past conflicts.
First Minister of Scotland John Swinney placed a wreath at the Stone of Remembrance outside the City Chambers during an event in Edinburgh.
Veterans, military personnel and cadets also marched through the centres of British cities such as Manchester, Birmingham and Leeds.
A silent poppy drop was held as part of the Festival of Remembrance at Durham Cathedral while wreaths were laid at Canterbury Cathedral.
Separately, the Duke of Sussex was seen attending a Remembrance service in the market town of Brackley in Northamptonshire.
For more than a century, the national Remembrance event has been held around the Cenotaph.
The monument was built as a focal point for honouring those who had fought and died in World War One, including those who had no grave, and as a place to mourn for those families who might not be able to visit war cemeteries overseas.
The word "cenotaph" means "empty tomb" in Greek and it was designed by the architect Sir Edwin Lutyens in a simple, austere style, with no sense of triumphalism and with almost no decoration.
The monument had been originally built in 1919 as a temporary, plaster and wood structure. But it proved so popular with the public that it was replaced in 1920 with a permanent version, in the same design but in stone.
It was opened at 11:00 on 11 November 1920 by King George V. His great-grandson, Charles, was there again, on an overcast morning 106 years later, to continue paying respect.

articles.title_orig: Chinese carmaker BYD’s offices in Netherlands raided over JLR ‘copycat car’ claim
articles.title_zh: Chinese carmaker BYD’s offices in Netherlands raided over JLR ‘copycat car’ claim
articles.content_orig:
Bailiffs reportedly seized digital records before court case over alleged intellectual property breaches on Land Rover Defender
Bailiffs acting for Jaguar Land Rover raided the Dutch offices of a Chinese “copycat” rival before a legal showdown this week over whether its “Defender clone” infringes intellectual property rights.
Bailiffs acting on behalf of JLR reportedly seized digital records from the offices of Chinese carmaker BYD in Schiedam and Hoofddorp in August, according to the Sunday Times.
The raid took place before a court case in the The Hague this week which will decide whether the BYD has a case to answer over allegations that its Ti7 SUV infringes the intellectual property of the Land Rover Defender.
Motoring experts have likened BYD’s seven-seat plug-in hybrid SUV to the Defender since it went on sale in China in September last year. The company is scheduled to launch the vehicle, which the BBC’s Top Gear magazine called the “Chinese Defender clone” , in the UK market in January at a price of £47,995, undercutting the Defender by more than £20,000.
BYD says on its website that “an unapologetically boxy profile delivers the imposing, chunky design that finds favour among SUV buyers, yet delivers a contemporary look”.
The price of JLR’s seven-seat Defender 110 starts from £68,465and is one of the country’s bestselling cars. The UK-based carmaker, which is owned by India’s Tata Motors, sold 29,500 Defenders to retail customers between July and September this year, compared with 25,370a year earlier.
The raid in the Netherlands was carried out by court-ordered bailiffs, with JLR suspecting that BYD reverse-engineered some of the technology that could be used in the Ti7, the Times reported. JLR wanted to secure the digital records before they could be destroyed.
JLR and BYD declined to comment on the “ongoing legal proceedings”.
The dispute with BYD is not the first legal case JLR has pursed against a Chinese company over copycat allegations. It won a legal case to stop Jiangling Motor Corporation selling a copycat vehicle in 2019 after a three-year court battle.
after newsletter promotion
In some cases JLR has taken a collaborative approach to dealing with the rise of China’s carmakers. It agreed to form a joint venture with Chery in a 2012 deal which later included licensing its discontinued Freelander brand with the company.
Chery’s Jaecoo model, which is not part of the joint venture, has been called the Temu Range Rover because of its similarities to the JLR vehicle after years of collaboration between the pair. It costs £10,000 less than JLR’s Range Rover.
The Jaecoo was the bestselling car in the UK in October, with 10,813 registrations, taking its market share from 2.07% to 4.30%, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers & Traders. JLR’s sales of the Range Rover fell to 43,300 in the third quarter of this year, from 47,196 cars sold in the same months last year.

articles.title_orig: Will Eisenkot be able to form Israel’s next gov’t amid divided opposition?
articles.title_zh: Will Eisenkot be able to form Israel’s next gov’t amid divided opposition?
articles.content_orig:
Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has been given the opportunity to form a new government after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s ruling coalition lost its parliamentary majority in the October elections, raising the possibility of an end to his long tenure in power.
President Isaac Herzog selected the former military chief on Saturday, following consultations with political parties. Eisenkot has 28 days to cobble together a coalition to form a government. If he fails to form a new administration within that period, he can seek a 14-day extension.
“Now is the time to form a national emergency government. I will do everything to ensure we are worthy,” Eisenkot, the leader of the Yashar party, posted on X.
However, the 66-year-old faces a difficult challenge as many of the opposition parties hold sharply conflicting positions on national security, religion and the Israeli occupation of Palestinian territory.
Neither Eisenkot nor Netanyahu has a 61-seat majority in Israel’s 120-member parliament, the Knesset.
As a result, Arab-led parties hold a potentially decisive role in determining who governs Israel, even as Eisenkot and his prospective partners refuse to rely on their support.
So what do we now know about Eisenkot’s possible paths to power, and can he succeed in unseating Netanyahu?
Eisenkot’s potential coalition spans his Yashar party, the centre-left Democrats led by Yair Golan, Naftali Bennett’s centre-right Together party and Avigdor Lieberman’s right-wing Yisrael Beiteinu (Israel Our Home).
Overall, they control 48 seats, well short of a majority.
Arab-led parties Ra’am (United List) and the Joint List (comprising three parties – Hadash, Ta’al and Balad) – jointly holding 19 seats – have endorsed Eisenkot’s attempt to form a government. Their backing would give the broader anti-Netanyahu camp a combined 67 seats.
Hadash is an Arab-Jewish party, Ta’al advocates for the rights of Palestinian citizens of Israel, and Balad demands equal rights for all its citizens.
However, Eisenkot has ruled out bringing Arab parties into his government, while Lieberman has repeatedly rejected forming a minority administration dependent on their support. Golan’s Democrats have been more willing to partner with Ra’am and the Joint List.
“We must no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes,” Golan said after the election.
Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist coalition has fallen from the 64 seats it secured in 2022 to 53, eight seats short of a majority.
His Likud is the largest individual party with 27 seats, while Eisenkot’s Yashar won 21.
Netanyahu’s efforts to remain in power suffered a further setback when United Torah Judaism, a longtime ultra-Orthodox ally, declined to endorse him or any other candidate during consultations with Herzog.
While the decision hurts Netanyahu’s prospects of regaining power, it did not rule out the party supporting him in future coalition negotiations if their demands were met, particularly compulsory military service for ultra-Orthodox Jews, which they reject.
If Eisenkot is unable to put together a coalition, he could potentially lead a minority government backed by Arab parties from outside.
A minority government is formed when the parties holding cabinet positions do not collectively control a majority of seats in parliament. Instead, they depend on support from lawmakers outside the governing coalition to remain in power and pass legislation.
Eisenkot could establish such an administration with his four-party bloc relying on external parliamentary support from Ra’am and the Joint List .
Under this arrangement, the Arab-led parties would not necessarily receive cabinet positions or formally join the coalition.
They could instead negotiate policy concessions in exchange for their parliamentary support.
In 2021, Ra’am joined a government led by Bennett, becoming the first independent Arab party to participate in an Israeli governing coalition.
That administration collapsed after 18 months, mainly due to disagreements over the illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank and Palestinian statehood. Most Israeli parties do not support the creation of a sovereign Palestinian state as part of the so-called two-state solution.
Netanyahu, who has been in power for most of the past 20 years, has openly rejected Palestinian statehood and has pushed settlement expansions that are the biggest hurdles in the realisation of Palestinian statehood. Settlements are considered illegal under international law.
Beyond a minority government, Eisenkot could attempt to secure a parliamentary majority by bringing Israel’s two ultra-Orthodox parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism, into his coalition.
Together, they hold 13 seats, which would give Eisenkot’s bloc exactly the 61 seats required for a majority.
However, such an alliance would require compromises over military conscription exemptions for ultra-Orthodox religious students, an issue that has long divided Israeli politics.
Eisenkot and his allies, particularly Lieberman, have criticised the exemptions. But Lieberman has recently indicated that he is open to compromise.
While United Torah Judaism has refused to endorse Netanyahu, Shas backed the beleaguered prime minister.
Another option would be a unity government involving Eisenkot’s Yashar, Bennett’s Together party, Lieberman’s Israel Our Home and Netanyahu’s Likud.
Such an alliance would command 67 seats, but would require Eisenkot and his partners to abandon their central election pledge to remove Netanyahu from power.
If Eisenkot fails to form a government within the required time, Herzog could give Netanyahu an opportunity to form a governing coalition.
Should both leaders fail, parliament could nominate another candidate. If no government emerges after a process lasting 100 days, Israelis could be heading to the polls again.
The negotiations could determine not only who becomes Israel’s next prime minister, but also which political parties control key ministries and shape policies on the economy, military conscription and the occupied Palestinian territory.
Several members of Eisenkot’s opposition bloc have previously held senior government positions, including in the coalition that removed Netanyahu from power in 2021.
Bennett, who served as prime minister from 2021 to 2022, has long opposed the establishment of a Palestinian state and advocated annexing large parts of the occupied West Bank.
During Israel’s 11-day war on Gaza in May 2021, Bennett, then an opposition politician, backed Netanyahu’s military offensive in the Palestinian enclave. More than 250 Palestinians were killed in Israeli attacks.

articles.title_orig: South Africa’s ANC suffers setback in local elections
articles.title_zh: South Africa’s ANC suffers setback in local elections
articles.content_orig:
South Africa’s African National Congress (ANC) party faces a major setback after last week’s municipal elections, leaving it in a weak position in coalition talks to form city governments.
With all votes counted on Sunday, President Cyril Ramaphosa’s ANC had just over 30 percent nationally against about 25 percent for its main rival, the Democratic Alliance (DA).
That represents a drop of roughly 14 percentage points from its 2021 local elections performance.
Former President Jacob Zuma’s uMkhonto weSizwe party won about 10 percent of votes, putting it in third place, while the rest of the ballots were split between hundreds of smaller parties.
While still the largest party in South Africa, the ANC’s support has steadily eroded as voters grow increasingly frustrated with corruption and the party’s failure to tackle unemployment, which tops 34 percent more than three decades after the end of apartheid.
Failures in basic services, such as water and electricity, have also contributed to the ANC’s vote share falling in local elections over the past 15 years.
The party failed to win an outright majority in any of the eight major metro areas, including Johannesburg and Pretoria.
Since no party won more than 50 percent of the votes in many cities, including South Africa’s commercial hub Johannesburg, the ANC and DA will have to team up or hash it out with smaller parties to form municipal governments.
Parties will have 14 days to negotiate before city councils are formed.
ANC Secretary-General Fikile Mbalula called the result “catastrophic” for the ANC but said the party would not go begging for positions when coalition talks begin soon.
“When the people tell us we have fallen short, … the honest answer is not to argue with them but to go home and put our house in order,” Mbalula said on Saturday.
In Johannesburg, the DA led the count with about 35 percent of the votes, compared with 20 percent for the ANC.
That could give DA veteran Helen Zille, who campaigned on fixing potholes and leaking water pipes, a good chance of becoming mayor, depending on the coalition agreements reached.
The DA said in a statement that it would initiate coalition discussions with “political parties that share a commitment to clean and accountable government, rooting out corruption, service delivery for all, the rule of law, and non-racialism”.

articles.title_zh: CEO SUNDAY: Army veteran turned health tech boss calls support for those who served a 'sacred obligation'
articles.content_orig:
Philips North America CEO Jeff DiLullo shares how his Army service shaped his leadership, career and commitment to supporting veterans.
Long after Jeff DiLullo traded his Army uniform for a suit, a lesson from his years at West Point and in the military has stayed with him: the importance of serving "something bigger" than himself.
As CEO of Philips North America, a global health technology company that makes medical equipment used in hospitals, DiLullo has found a new way to put that lesson into practice through his work supporting veterans and their families.
"One of the most rewarding things for me personally that I've brought from my military service into my corporate life is a sense of service and serving something bigger than myself," DiLullo told FOX Business. "And now today, I do that through serving our veteran community."
BUILT FROM SCRATCH: HOW A RENTED KITCHEN AND HAND-SQUEEZED FRUIT BECAME A VERSATILE MIXER
He added, "To me, it's a sacred obligation as a nation to serve our veterans and not only them, but their families and caregivers too."
DiLullo graduated from the United States Military Academy at West Point with a bachelor's degree in history before serving as an infantry officer in the U.S. Army. He later earned an MBA in marketing , logistics and supply chain from the University of Tennessee's Haslam College of Business.
GOOGLE PARTNERS WITH VETERANS GROUPS TO HELP 25,000 ENTER SKILLED TRADES CAREERS AMID WORKER SHORTAGE
As CEO of Philips North America, DiLullo has found a new way to put that lesson into practice through his work supporting veterans and their families. (Philips North America)
His connection to military service has only become more personal in recent years. DiLullo's daughter and son-in-law are both currently on active duty, and he knows firsthand that eventually leaving the military can bring its own challenges.
"When you leave the military, you wonder if you're going to maintain the connection to a mission and something important and purposeful," DiLullo said. "Many veterans struggle with that transition just like I did."
After leaving the Army, he built a successful career in corporate America, eventually holding executive leadership positions at Hewlett-Packard, Avaya and Dell.
"After the Army, honestly, I buried myself in work," he said. "I tried to find a sense of purpose and mission in what I was doing, and I had great jobs, but I hit a wall, and I was trying to do everything well but not feeling that I was really deeply connected to my own sense of purpose."
The realization ultimately pushed him to rethink what he wanted from his career.
"After a period of reflection, almost 10 years ago, I decided to just change course completely," he said. "I moved into healthcare and I decided I would only work where I felt a personal sense of purpose, and I have never looked back. I'm having the most fun I've had in my entire career."
VETERAN-OWNED TEA COMPANY AIMS TO HELP FORMER SERVICE MEMBERS ‘FIND PURPOSE’
DiLullo joined Philips in 2019 as head of North America operations.
That path eventually brought DiLullo to Philips, where he joined the company in 2019 as head of North America operations. His responsibilities expanded in 2021 to include leadership of the company's North America services and solutions delivery teams.
Today, DiLullo said his work has given him a renewed connection to the sense of mission he valued in the military.
The Department of Veterans Affairs is Philips' largest customer , according to DiLullo, and he also serves on the board of the Elizabeth Dole Foundation, which supports military and veteran caregivers.
"These things are fuel for me and really fuel my sense of purpose and connection and service," he said.
Asked what advice he would offer today's West Point cadets, DiLullo said their commitment to the country does not have to end when their military careers do.
"You've taken a solemn vow to serve and defend your nation ," he said. "You have willingly taken up the responsibility to protect the freedoms that are the foundation of this great country."
DiLullo added, "Service does not end when you leave the military. Your oath is to a lifetime of service to the nation. So my advice will be always to know and serve something bigger than yourself."
VETERANS ARE USING THIS HOMEBUYING BENEFIT MORE OFTEN — BUT MANY STILL DON’T KNOW IT EXISTS
DiLullo graduated from the United States Military Academy at West Point with a bachelor's degree in history before serving as an infantry officer in the U.S. Army. (Rich Graessle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)
Among all the roles DiLullo has held since leaving the military, one still stands apart.

"I can honestly say, other than the military, this is the most fulfilling work I've ever done," he said of his work in healthcare.
But the best job he ever had?
"The best job I ever had was the Army," DiLullo said. "A sense of mission, teamwork, and trust. It just defined my ideal world."

articles.content_orig:

Who is winning the AI race between the United States and China? The answer depends on what you measure.
Photo: Jason Edwards/Getty
Asia Power Snapshot: China, the United States, and the race for AI dominance
US President Donald Trump has declared that “whoever wins AI wins,” suggesting that the competition for mastery over artificial intelligence (AI) is the pre-eminent geopolitical contest of the day. But who is winning the AI race between the United States and China? The answer depends on what you measure. This Data Snapshot compares the inputs and outputs that matter most — from chips and compute to research and innovation — to show which side holds the lead, where the gaps are narrowing, and where capabilities may be overstated.
Based on a thorough analysis of available data, including 14 indicators across four measures — Resources, Technology, AI capabilities, and AI adoption — the United States is currently leading the race. However, its lead is far from uniform, and the competition remains uneven across multiple domains. The United States is well ahead in AI capabilities, driven by its dominance in compute, and in AI adoption, where its lead in web traffic and apps outweighs China’s edge in open models. By contrast, China has a clear lead in Resources, particularly critical minerals — the key materials needed for manufacturing the advanced technologies that make AI possible. Governance, however, remains contested. Neither superpower is widely trusted to regulate AI, leaving room for middle powers such as Australia to help shape the rules.
China holds a clear advantage over the United States in both production and known reserves of critical minerals.
In November 2025, the US Department of the Interior released a list of 60 minerals critical to its economic and national security interests. 1 China leads in production of 30, while the United States is ahead in only eight — with 22 not produced in either country. China holds larger known reserves of 20 listed minerals, and the United States of seven, with one tied, and insufficient data for the remaining 32.
China’s ability to impose targeted export controls on critical minerals poses a major risk for the United States. In 2023, Beijing began announcing restrictions on several, including gallium and germanium — both used in semiconductors. 2
To counter this vulnerability, the United States has sought to cooperate with other countries to secure critical minerals. It has developed Pax Silica, a 24-member international framework focused on AI-related supply chain resilience. 3 In Asia, it has critical minerals frameworks with Australia and Japan and has also signed memoranda of understanding with Malaysia and Thailand. 4 In February 2026, it held a Critical Minerals Ministerial meeting, where it signed an additional 11 bilateral agreements, including one with the Philippines. 5
* For more on the semiconductor supply chain in Asia, and Southeast Asia’s role as a connector between the United States and China, see Between the superpowers: Southeast Asia’s strategic supply chain dilemma (Opens in new window) .
The United States leads China in technological sophistication. While China has almost 11 million full-time equivalent researchers — over seven million more than the United States — US spending on research and development (R&D) is considerably higher as a share of GDP (3.45 per cent versus China’s 2.58 per cent). The United States also has a sizeable lead in the number of data centres and supercomputers.
The United States has sought to limit China’s access to advanced technologies that could help develop its semiconductor industry. Washington has imposed numerous restrictions on both China and Chinese subsidiaries abroad, which has, in turn, spurred affected companies to innovate around them. 6 In May 2026, Huawei announced a new chip-design approach intended to increase transistor density without shrinking transistors. This could allow it to design chips by 2031 with transistor density equivalent to that of the chips Taiwan’s TSMC aims to make in 2028, without the advanced lithography machines China is barred from importing. 7 If successful, this could limit the effect of US export controls.
While companies have looked for ways to work around US controls, Beijing has moved to expand its own, building on its critical mineral restrictions. In October 2026, China proposed adding 40 technologies to its restricted exports, including 23 related to AI — among them AI chip design, the core technology of the most advanced models, and AI tools, such as deepfake detection systems. 8
The United States maintains a lead in AI capabilities. Its AI data centres have nearly 40 times the combined computing power of China’s, and its AI chips 31 times. This has helped US models stay ahead in benchmark tests, though the margin is narrowing.
As of November 2026, the top US large language model (LLM) on Arena, a platform that ranks models through blind head-to-head comparisons, is Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon, with an estimated score of 1528, closely followed by Google’s Gemini 4 Argon at 1520 and Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 at 1509. China’s top model, Moonshot’s Kimi K3, released in mid-July 2026, scores an estimated 1488, placing it 19th. The last top US model at this level was Google’s Gemini 3 Pro, which led from its release in mid-November 2025 until late January 2026. This gap is consistent with claims that the United States has a six-to-nine-month lead in AI capabilities. 9
The global spread of LLMs is arguably the most important front in the AI race. The models that consumers, businesses, and governments rely on will shape the information they see, how their economies run, and, potentially, the future of war. Which country leads depends on how users access the models.
There are six main ways to do so:
Reliable data exist for four of these: websites, apps, self-hosted open models, and aggregator platforms.
China holds a comfortable lead in self-hosted open models and aggregator platforms. 10 In the third quarter of 2026, Chinese models were downloaded nearly 1.8 billion times on Hugging Face, compared with 500 million for US models, giving China 78 per cent of the two countries’ combined downloads. Such models particularly appeal to governments and businesses, which can run them on their own servers to keep data local and adapt them to their needs. On aggregator platform OpenRouter, Chinese models accounted for 55 per cent of all text requests in the week commencing 26 October 2026 — compared to the US share of 38 per cent.
However, most users access LLMs through websites, apps, and embedded AI. The United States has a commanding lead in websites and apps. US models drew more than 90 per cent of combined global traffic to US and Chinese AI websites. US models also accounted for more than 80 per cent of combined use of US and Chinese AI apps, based on Google Play downloads and, for China, where Google Play is unavailable, QuestMobile data.
Overall, most people who use AI rely on US models, giving the United States unmatched reach and greater influence over the technology’s global direction.
With no other country posing a challenge to their dominance in AI, the United States and China have an outsized influence over how the technology is governed globally.
Rival blocs are already taking shape. Washington launched Pax Silica in December 2025 to secure AI supply chains among trusted partners. Beijing answered in July 2026 with the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO), which centres on AI governance standards and digital development. articles.title_orig: New Zealand dairy giant Fonterra speeds up China innovation
articles.title_zh: New Zealand dairy giant Fonterra speeds up China innovation
articles.content_orig:
Fonterra Co-operative Group Ltd is accelerating product development with Chinese customers as the New Zealand dairy giant seeks to capture growing demand for protein-rich foods and dairy products tailored to local tastes.
The company is leveraging its six application centers in China to help bakeries, beverage chains and food manufacturers bring new products to market faster, supported by investments in production capacity in New Zealand, CEO Richard Allen said in an interview during the China International Import Expo in Shanghai.
"We know how fast the China market moves and how quickly trends change," Allen said. "Alongside our customers, we can work with them to create new products with new selling points."
A recent visit to Chengdu, Sichuan province, highlighted how much the market had evolved since he worked in China's foodservice sector many years ago.
Allen said dairy products had become more prominent in bakeries, supermarkets and membership stores, with a growing number of products emphasizing their protein content.
Chinese food and beverage brands are also increasingly highlighting the grass-fed origins of New Zealand dairy ingredients to differentiate their products and strengthen their premium positioning.
However, turning those attributes into sales requires products that deliver both quality and value.
Fonterra works with customers to select ingredients that meet nutritional and taste requirements while keeping costs affordable for consumers and commercially viable for producers, Allen said.
"You've got to have nutrition, but it also has to taste good," he said.
Its six application centers in China bring together chefs, marketing specialists and sales teams to develop products suited to local and regional tastes.
For one bakery customer, Fonterra explored incorporating Sichuan's signature mala, or spicy and numbing, flavors into baked goods. Allen also cited the pairing of Anchor butter with pineapple buns as an example of how dairy ingredients can be incorporated into established local food traditions.
"By being on the ground, close to our customers, to their consumers, it allows us to work every day with our customers on developing new products very quickly," he said.
China is also becoming a source of product innovation for Fonterra's operations elsewhere in Asia.
Dairy-topped tea drinks developed in China, for example, have created opportunities among the company's foodservice customers in Southeast Asia, Allen said.
Meanwhile, the overseas expansion of Chinese restaurant and beverage chains is opening another avenue for growth.
As these brands enter international markets, they increasingly seek consistent supplies of familiar ingredients to maintain product quality and taste across their global operations.
Fonterra is supporting Chinese customers expanding into Southeast Asia, the United States, Europe, Australia and New Zealand, drawing on its international supply network and foodservice expertise.
"Not only can we support our local customers in other markets, but we can support Chinese brands in accessing other markets," Allen said.
The strategy builds on Fonterra's established ingredients and foodservice businesses in China, where the cooperative has operated for nearly five decades.
Allen described China as one of Fonterra's cornerstone markets, with demand for dairy ingredients and nutritional products continuing to create opportunities for long-term growth.
To support that demand, Fonterra is investing NZ$150 million ($87 million) to expand ultra-high-temperature cream production at its Edendale facility in New Zealand.
The additional capacity will serve customers in China and other markets, complementing investments in local application centers and culinary, marketing and sales teams.
The expansion comes as Fonterra reported stronger financial results for the year ended July 2026. The cooperative posted revenue of NZ$27 billion and total group operating profit of NZ$3.4 billion in results released on Sept 24.
Fonterra has also announced an additional NZ$1 billion investment over three years to expand its protein manufacturing network in New Zealand's South Island and improve environmental performance.
In China, Allen sees further opportunities in protein-rich products. During his visits to Chinese supermarkets, he was struck by the growing number of products promoting their protein content.
"For us, being agile and moving fast, and ensuring our customers are agile and moving fast, is about being close to the market and really understanding what's happening," Allen said.

Russian leader Vladimir Putin has placed three additional subsidiaries of Japan Tobacco International (JTI) under Russian-appointed management, expanding Moscow’s takeover of the Japanese tobacco giant’s operations to seven companies, with the affected assets valued at up to $3.7 billion.

According to The Moscow Times on November 7, the latest presidential decree transferred control of JTI Russia, Pereslavl-Tabak, and JTI Innovative Products to the Russian company Industrial Assets.
The decision follows a separate decree issued on November 5 that placed four JTI manufacturing and tobacco-related businesses under the same management structure.
Bloomberg reported that the newly affected companies include a holding entity, a cigarette distribution business, and an importer of electronic tobacco products and heated tobacco systems.
The earlier takeover covered Petro, JTI Donskoy Tabak, Kres Neva, and JTI Yelets, which collectively employ approximately 4,000 people. According to The Moscow Times, Russian industry analysts estimate the combined value of the affected assets at 250 billion to 300 billion rubles, or approximately $3.1 billion to $3.7 billion.
Industrial Assets was established in September 2026. Russian corporate records identify Sergei Dremov, a former member of the State Council of Russian-occupied Crimea, as one of its founders. His biography indicates that he served in Russian state security agencies between 2000 and 2016.
